Mozart → The Beatles · how the training pipeline works

The LLM Playbook

On this page, we apply the LLM playbook to music.

? Why Music?

Music is the perfect playground for learning about LLMs — public-domain data, a vocabulary of 12 notes instead of tens of thousands of sub-words, and a full training run that fits on a home GPU in hours instead of a data center for weeks.

Listen to whether rock-preference fine-tuning actually sounds more rock-like.

Card #24/#28's own quantitative verdict on this run: chosen vs. rejected P(rock) diverged during training as designed, but genuine distance to a real rock centroid did not improve, and the biggest classifier-score gains traced back to the model exploiting a documented multicollinearity quirk, not to sounding more like rock. Listen for yourself — this is a cautionary tale about optimizing a classifier, not a demonstrated win.

Same real G-G-G-E♭ motif prompt used everywhere else on this page, now continued by the rock-preference fine-tune instead of a composer adapter.

Notes pending — commentary to follow.

A different kind of intermediate signal: instead of predicting notes directly, could the model first predict a short “reasoning trace” — a MOTIF/CADENCE/SEQUENCE label — and use that as scratch space before committing to real notes? The same idea as chain-of-thought prompting in text LLMs, applied to music: 10 reasoning-token ids interleaved into the training sequence, SFT (plain next-token cross-entropy, not RL) on top of the frozen Phase 1 checkpoint.

Round 1: a real bug, found and fixed

The first run trained cleanly (val_loss 3.4587→3.0927) but generated almost nothing — 16 of 18 samples decoded to 0–1 real notes. Root cause, found by direct inspection rather than guessed: the tokenizer's real runtime vocabulary is BPE-trained up to 4,000 slots, and the reasoning ids (700–709) had been placed inside that live range. The decode step was stripping everything ≥564 to remove reasoning tokens — but ids 564–3999 are ~85% of the real vocabulary, so it was discarding almost all real note content too. Fixed the same way this project already fixed an identical class of bug for System 2: resize the vocab (4000→4010), move the reasoning ids to 4000–4009, retrain from scratch. Generation went from 2/18 audible samples to 18/18, 40–66 real notes each.

Round 2: does the reasoning signal actually help? A real, rigorous “no”

At n=8, the first fixed run looked promising — forcing a repeated motif token (MOTIF_REPEAT) beat a matched control (MOTIF_NEW, same shape and position, different class) by +64% on a structural-self-similarity metric. That result did not survive a proper retest with real confidence intervals: at higher statistical power, conditioned / matched-control / baseline are not distinguishable from each other on either metric. The n=8 comparison's apparent win was noise, not a real effect of the reasoning-token class — reported here exactly that plainly, since finding out an early positive result doesn't replicate is itself a real, useful finding for this project.

What did turn out to be real: a duration bias, unrelated to reasoning at all

Every arm — conditioned, matched control, and the plain unconstrained baseline — shows the same thing: the model's own predicted note durations sit 25–45% below the real training corpus's average, independent of temperature and independent of which reasoning token (if any) was injected. That's a genuine learned bias in the base model, not something the reasoning-token mechanism caused or can fix — an unplanned discovery that came out of testing the reasoning-trace hypothesis, not the hypothesis itself.

What it actually sounds like, post-fix

One real sample from the fixed run — step 60 of 300, seed 1, 47 real notes, 13.9s. Real audio, real REMI decode, no cherry-picking beyond “this is the seed used elsewhere on this page.”

seed 1 · 47 real notes · 13.9s

A separate thread from the pipeline above: instead of one model generating alone, could two GPT “voices” trade phrases, the way musicians trade fours? System 2 is a small planner that sketches a chord/rhythm/tempo progression ahead of time. System 1 is a LoRA-tuned version of this project's own Pretraining checkpoint that fills in real notes conditioned on that plan. Both clips below are a one-shot setup: System 2 writes its plan once, upfront, and System 1 just plays through it start to finish — neither model reacts to what's actually being played, yet.

System 2 (original) — plan once, generate straight through

System 3 — one-shot baseline (same idea, later pipeline)

Still a static plan (System 2 doesn't react mid-piece here either), but run through System 3's later, gap-fixed pipeline — the fairest direct comparator to System 2's original clip above, since it isolates pipeline maturity from the turn-taking question itself.
